entities.summary:
The 'Death of a Salesman' is a seminal American stage play written by Arthur Miller that premiered on February 10, 1949, at the Morosco Theatre on Broadway, New York City. Set against the backdrop of post-World War II America, it intricately explores the struggles of Willy Loman, a traveling salesman who grapples with the elusive nature of the American Dream in a rapidly changing society. This play not only broke new ground in American theater but also resonated globally, reflecting universal themes of identity, success, and disillusionment that transcend geographical boundaries.

The narrative unfolds in a two-act structure, weaving together Willy Loman's present-day failures with flashbacks of his past. Over 742 performances, audiences witnessed Willy's tragic decline, driven by his aspirations and the societal pressures of the late 1940s. The character's poignant encounters with his family, particularly his sons Biff and Happy, illustrate the generational conflict and the weight of unmet expectations. Miller's work is steeped in realism, using the city of Brooklyn as a microcosm for broader societal issues, including capitalism's moral dilemmas and the psychological burdens of self-worth.

The legacy of 'Death of a Salesman' is profound, as it has influenced countless playwrights, directors, and actors worldwide, solidifying Arthur Miller's status as a pivotal figure in American theater. The play's critical examination of the American Dream has sparked dialogues that continue to resonate, especially in discussions about socioeconomic disparities and mental health. It paved the way for subsequent works that challenge traditional narratives, inspiring movements that seek to address the human condition and societal expectations.

Their legacy is studied through the lens of historical causation.", "summary": "Death of a Salesman is the play by Arthur Miller (1915–2005), which premiered on Broadway at the Morosco Theatre on 10 February 1949 (directed by Elia Kazan, with Lee J. Cobb as Willy Loman) and won the Pulitzer Prize for Drama and the Tony Award for Best Play — one of the most celebrated and widely performed plays in the American theatrical canon and a foundational text in the critique of the American Dream. Its protagonist, Willy Loman, is a 63-year-old travelling salesman in Brooklyn whose career is collapsing, whose sons have failed to live up to his expectations, and who lives in a world of delusion and memory — the play moving between present and past in an innovative expressionistic structure in which Willy's memories and fantasies break into the action of the present — until Willy kills himself in a car 'accident', hoping that the life insurance payment will give his son Biff the money to succeed in business. The play's famous last lines, spoken by Linda at Willy's poorly attended funeral — 'We're free... We're free...' — are devastating in their irony.

Death of a Salesman is a tragedy in the classical sense — the downfall of a man whose fatal flaw is his devotion to an illusion (the American Dream of success through personal attractiveness and salesmanship) — but Miller wrote it as a 'tragedy of the common man', arguing in his famous essay 'Tragedy and the Common Man' (1949) that the ordinary person is as fit a subject for tragedy as the kings and heroes of classical drama. Willy Loman's surname ('Lo-man' — low man) is one of the most famous bits of symbolism in American drama: the man at the bottom of the social hierarchy whose aspirations, delusions, and dignity are those of every salesman, every father, every person who has invested their self-worth in the image others have of them.
